6                 IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                    
7                     FOR THE DISTRICT OF ARIZONA                        

8                                                                        

9   BBK Tobacco & Foods LLP,           No. CV-19-05216-PHX-MTL           

10              Plaintiff,              ORDER                             

11   v.                                                                   
                                       NOT FOR PUBLICATION               
12   Central Coast Agriculture Incorporated, et                           
    al.,                                                                 
13                                                                        
               Defendants.                                               
14                                                                        
15        Before the Court is the parties’ Joint Notice of Discovery Dispute. (Doc. 266.) 
16   Plaintiff BBK Tobacco & Foods LLP (“BBK”) seeks to depose certain non-testifying 
17   expert  consultants  retained  by  Defendant  Central  Coast  Agriculture  Incorporated 
18   (“CCA”). For the reasons that follow, the Court resolves the dispute in BBK’s favor and 
19   will permit the depositions.                                         
20                                   I.                                   
21        In response to initial expert reports served by BBK, CCA retained a firm named 
22   MFour to conduct a rebuttal survey measuring “CA cannabis consumers[’] (concentrate 
23   consumers specifically) level of care when purchasing Cannabis products” and measuring 
24   “consumer[s’] understanding of Raw Garden and perceived affiliated brands.” (Doc. 273-
25   1 at 6, 19, 28). The survey instrument and results were delivered to CCA’s rebuttal 
26   testifying experts and to BBK. BBK was also provided with an authenticating declaration 
27   from MFour’s Co-Founder and Chief Operating Officer, Jeff Harrelson. (Doc. 273 at 2.)  
28        CCA’s testifying experts, Dr. Erdem and Dr. Honka, rely heavily on the survey data. 
1   (See Doc. 274-1 ¶¶ 40, 44, 46–47; Doc. 206-36 ¶¶ 28–30.) But neither testifying expert 
2   was involved in the survey’s design or administration or has knowledge as to how the 
3   survey was designed or administered. (Doc. 274 at 3–5.) Upon learning as much, BBK 
4   requested to depose someone from MFour with such knowledge. After initially objecting, 
5   CCA eventually agreed to work with BBK to facilitate the deposition of Mr. Harrelson. 
6   (See Doc. 266-2.) At the deposition, Mr. Harrelson testified that he, too, lacked knowledge 
7   as to how to the survey was designed or conducted. (See id. at 5, 21–22, 34–38.) Mr. 
8   Harrelson did, however, identify the two MFour employees that designed and conducted 
9   the survey—Ms. Lindsay Fawcett and Ms. Allyson Wehn. (Id. at 21–22, 28–29.)  
10        BBK now seeks to depose Ms. Fawcett and Ms. Wehn. CCA objects.  
11                                  II.                                   
12        “Ordinarily, a party may not, by interrogatories or deposition, discover facts known 
13   or opinions held by an expert who has been retained . . . and who is not expected to be 
14   called as a witness at trial. But a party may do so . . . on showing exceptional circumstances 
15   under which it is impracticable for the party to obtain facts or opinions on the same subject 
16   by other means.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(4)(D).                        
17        Exceptional circumstances are present here. See Pinal Creek Grp. v. Newmont Min. 
18   Corp., No. CV-91-1764-PHX-DAE, 2006 WL 1817000, at *6 (D. Ariz. June 30, 2006) 
19   (“[E]xceptional circumstances ha[ve] been shown where a non-testifying expert’s report 
20   will be used by a testifying expert as the basis for an expert opinion.”). While CCA has 
21   provided BBK with the survey questionnaire and raw data results, BBK has been unable to 
22   obtain information regarding the survey’s design and methodology. BBK has exhaustively 
23   attempted to obtain this information by means other than deposing the non-testifying 
24   consultant  experts  but  has  been  unsuccessful.  And  BBK  must  have  access  to  this 
25   information to reasonably test the survey’s admissibility and reliability.  
26        Pakootas v. Teck Cominco Metals, a 2011 case out of the Eastern District of 
27   Washington,  involved  a  similar  discovery  dispute  to  the  one  presented  here,  and  is 
28   instructive:                                                         
1             The non-testifying consultant experts whom Plaintiff seeks to 
              depose have engaged in original research and developed data 
2                                                                        
              pertinent to specific issues in this case which are relied upon 
3             by experts who intend to testify on behalf of the Defendant. 
              They are not consultants who have done no more than offer  
4                                                                        
              advice to a litigating party based on expertise in a relevant 
5             field. Defendant’s testifying experts explicitly rely on certain 
              foundational information which has been developed by these 
6                                                                        
              non-testifying  consultant  experts.  This  information  is  not 
7             privileged or protectable as attorney work product and it would 
              be unfair to Plaintiff to not allow it to depose the non-testifying 
8                                                                        
              consultant experts.                                        
9                                                                        
    Pakootas v. Teck Cominco Metals, Ltd., No. CV-04-256-LRS, 2011 WL 13113380, at *1 
10                                                                        
    (E.D. Wash. July 7, 2011). So too here. CCA’s experts relied extensively on the MFour 
11                                                                        
12   survey in forming their opinions, and it would be unjust to preclude BBK from deposing 
13                                                                        
    the non-testifying consulting experts who designed and conducted the survey.  
14                                                                        
         CCA’s arguments in opposition are not persuasive. In essence, CCA contends that 
15                                                                        
16   the survey “is self-explanatory as to its reliability,” and that BBK’s expert should be able 
17                                                                        
    to identify any deficiencies merely by examining the survey questionnaire and raw data 
18                                                                        
    results. (Doc. 273 at 11.) But the law is not so restrictive. See, e.g., In re ConAgra Foods, 
19                                                                        
20   Inc., 90 F. Supp. 3d 919, 951–52 (C.D. Cal. 2015). Moreover, as BBK notes, “[a]ny 
21   suggestion that these necessary facts are evident from the survey itself is belied by CCA’s 
22                                                                        
    experts’ admissions that the facts are unknown, and by the inability of Mr. Harrelson to 
23                                                                        
    discern them from documents he purports to authenticate.” (Doc. 274 at 8.) 
24                                                                        
25        Accordingly,                                                    
26                                                                        
         IT IS ORDERED resolving the Joint Notice of Discovery Dispute dated December 
27                                                                        
    7, 2021 (Doc. 266) in BBK’s favor as described herein. BBK may depose Ms. Fawcett and 
28                                                                        
 ! ||  Ms. Wehn, or other person(s) designated by MFour that have knowledge of the survey’s 
2 
     design and methodology. These limited depositions may be conducted notwithstanding the 
3 
4    December 10, 2021  expert deposition deadline set forth in the Court’s Scheduling Order 
       (Doc. 31). Additional discovery is not permitted. 
6          IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that BBK shall conduct the requisite depositions by 
7 
g    no later than January 28, 2022. 
9          IT  IS  FURTHER  ORDERED  that  the  deadline  for  dispositive  motions  and 
1011    motions challenging expert opinion testimony to be filed is hereby extended to February 
11 
     11, 2022. 
12 
13          IT IS FINALLY ORDERED that each party shall bear its own fees and costs in 
      connection with this notice of discovery dispute. 
15 
                 Dated this 5th day of January, 2022. 
16 
17 
18                                           .                           . 
19                                     Michal  T.  dhunde 
50                                                 Michael T. Liburdi 
                                              United  States District Judge
